title: Measuring Product-Market Fit
intro: One question, from Sean Ellis: “How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?”

learn.title: The 40% benchmark
learn.text:
If **40% or more** of real, recent users answer **“very disappointed”**, you're likely on track.

Ignore the “somewhat disappointed” group — to them you're a nice-to-have.

Ellis himself calls 40% a target to aim for, not a magic line: a leading indicator, not a certificate.

try.q: Which answer group does the benchmark count?

learn.title: Who to ask
learn.text:
Survey people who have used the product **recently and meaningfully** — not everyone on the list.

An inactive user's answer tells you about your churn, not your fit. Mixing them in moves the number without telling you anything you can act on.

Ellis's own example: a startup scored **7%**, made targeted changes, and reached **40%** two weeks later.

try.q: A startup scores 7% and reaches 40% two weeks later. What does that show?
options: The score responds to targeted changes
Two weeks is the right interval
Product-market fit is easy to reach quickly
try.explain: It's a leading indicator you can move, not a fixed property.

learn.title: The follow-up questions
learn.text:
The survey points you at **whom to learn from**, not why.

Follow up with the “very disappointed” group:

• What is the main benefit you get?
• Who else would benefit from this?
• How could we improve it for you?
• What would you use instead?

Then triangulate with usage data and interviews.

try.q: What does the survey itself not tell you?
try.explain: It identifies whom to interview next.

test.explain: Widely used as a product-market fit signal.

options: How would you feel if you could no longer use this?
